searches.note: The three shared searches read the withdrawals of 2021 and 2022, the reasons Cheval Blanc and Ausone gave, and the 1955 classification for Cheval Blanc, Ausone and Figeac together. Two searches came back empty (one on the Pétrus clay in French words, one on Thierry Manoncourt in French that found the town of Figeac in the Lot) and are counted. Five of the share were left unspent. WebFetch was not tried.

method: The group was written with no web search, resting on the Codex library and the author's memory of the Oxford Companion and the World Atlas, neither opened. This recheck searched every fact beyond the Codex, strongest claims first: the people and their dates, the classification, the sales, the sites, the grapes, the making and its months, the label words and each beat of the story.

The Codex library and the two books are taken off every record's sources; each record now cites five pages a search returned, read: search, the estates' own domains marked primary where the summary came from them (Cheval Blanc and Figeac).

A fact found in two independent sources or one primary stands; a fact in one secondary only, or nowhere, is softened or taken out and listed here. A dead person whose dates were not found in two sources is described or, for Madame Loubat, whom the plan names, dated by her death alone.

The rules were tried on every string: no living person named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash; the questions for one right answer, plausible distractors and an explanation that teaches. Two label lines, Mis en bouteille au château for Cheval Blanc and Ausone, are taken off because no label was seen.

tested: The gold medal at the Paris Universal Exhibition of 1878 and the Arnaud family as owners from the late eighteenth century (Wikipedia, Decanter): confirmed.

Madame Loubat: shares from 1925 in two accounts and 1923 in one, sole owner by 1940, 1945 or 1949 by different accounts, a hotel keeper in Libourne, died 1961 (Wikipedia, Decanter, Waddingtons, the Wine Doctor): confirmed as the mid 1920s, the 1940s and 1961; her birth in 1877 as Marie-Louise Garitey rests on the Wine Doctor alone, and Edmonde is in other accounts her husband's name.

Jean-Pierre Moueix 1913 to 2003 (SommSelect, Decanter's report of his death aged 90 in 2003): confirmed; his sole right to sell is 1943 (Decanter), 1945 (Wikipedia) or 1947 (another account), so the record says the 1940s.
The frost of 1956 and the vines cut back to regrow on their old roots rather than replanted (Decanter, the Wine Doctor): confirmed; February is in no summary read and is cut.

The Moueix purchase of a share from the heirs in 1964 (Decanter, Wikipedia): confirmed. The Gazin parcel: 1969 in Wikipedia on Pétrus and Best of Wines, 1970 in Wikipedia on Gazin: kept as around 1970.

The clay: dense, dark blue, iron rich smectite that swells when wet, blocks water and resists roots, at the high point of the plateau (Wine Folly, SommSelect): confirmed; crasse de fer under it was not tied to Pétrus by any source and is cut.

The making: afternoon picking once the dew has dried (sommelier-academy and one other), concrete vats, eighteen to twenty months in oak with about half new in most accounts (others give twelve to eighteen months, or all new in the 1980s): confirmed as written now; the large picking team is cut.

The label of Saint Peter with the keys of heaven, commissioned by Madame Loubat in the 1940s (Waddingtons, 88 Bamboo): confirmed; the origin of the name itself is called uncertain, so the record says only that it is the Latin for Peter.
No second wine (Fine and Rare, Xtrawine): confirmed. The 1947 as a vintage of history (iDealwine, Hameau Albert): confirmed.

The rules: no living person named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash: sound. The question's options are now four titled widows, the key Madame Loubat, so the lint notes each title without a date.

changed.was: At the Universal Exhibition in Paris in 1878 a Pomerol wine won a gold medal, an early sign of fame for a commune the brokers of 1855 had passed over: Pétrus, then the property of the Arnaud family, named for Saint Peter, whose portrait with the keys of heaven appears on every label. From 1925 Madame Edmonde Loubat, who kept a hotel in Libourne and died in 1961, bought into the estate, and over the next two decades she gathered it into her own hands. After the Second World War she gave the young Libourne merchant Jean-Pierre Moueix (1913 to 2003) the sole right to sell the wine, and the 1947 that followed is a vintage of history. When the frost of February 1956 killed vines across the Right Bank, the estate cut its vines back to the stock rather than pull them up, as the story is told, and so kept their age. After Madame Loubat's death the Moueix family bought a share from her heirs, and in 1969 a parcel of neighbouring Château Gazin joined the vineyard. Pomerol never drew up a ranking, and Pétrus has never needed one: its standing rests on the clay, the Merlot and the care of one family of merchants.
changed.now: At the Universal Exhibition in Paris in 1878 a Pomerol wine won a gold medal, an early sign of fame for a commune the brokers of 1855 had passed over: Pétrus, then the property of the Arnaud family; its name is the Latin for Peter. From the mid 1920s Madame Loubat, who kept a hotel in Libourne and died in 1961, bought shares in the estate, and by the 1940s she held all of it and had given it the label that shows Saint Peter holding the keys of heaven. In the same decade she gave the Libourne merchant Jean-Pierre Moueix (1913 to 2003) the sole right to sell the wine, and the 1947 is a vintage of history. When the frost of 1956 killed vines across the Right Bank, she had the estate's vines cut back to grow again from their old roots rather than pulled up and replanted, and so kept their age. In 1964 the Moueix family bought a share from her heirs, and around 1970 a parcel bought from neighbouring Château Gazin joined the vineyard. Pomerol never drew up a ranking, and Pétrus has never needed one: its standing rests on the clay, the Merlot and the care of one family of merchants.
changed.why: The name is the Latin for Peter, its origin uncertain; Edmonde is cut as her husband's name in other accounts; the years of her shares and her sole ownership, and of the sole right to sell, differ between accounts and are given by their decades; the vines were cut back to their old roots; the Moueix share is dated 1964 and the Gazin parcel around 1970.

changed.was: A single pine tree beside a modest house gave Le Pin its name. The Thienpont family, wine merchants from Belgium, had owned Vieux Château Certan on the Pomerol plateau since 1924, and in 1979 a branch of the family bought this small plot nearby and named the new estate after the tree. The first vintage was made that same autumn, and from the start the wine went into new oak barrels, where it also finished its malolactic fermentation. The early vintages, the 1982 among them, were rich, ripe and ready young, and merchants in Britain and America were soon competing for the little there was. When winemakers in Saint-Émilion began in the 1990s to make tiny quantities of dense, new oaked wine in sheds and garages, writers called them garagistes, and Le Pin was named as their forerunner. The estate stayed small and never sought a rank: Pomerol has no classification, and Le Pin has made its name without one. In 2011 the family opened a new cellar beside the old house. It stands for the opulent side of Pomerol, the wine to pour when a guest wants pleasure young rather than in twenty years.
changed.now: A pine tree beside a modest house gave Le Pin its name. The Thienpont family, wine merchants from Belgium, had owned Vieux Château Certan on the Pomerol plateau since 1924, and in 1979 members of the family bought this small plot nearby, with its house and a small cellar. The first vintage was made that autumn in those rough surroundings and raised in old barrels from Vieux Château Certan; malolactic fermentation in barrel, begun when there were too few vats, became a habit of the house. The early vintages sold slowly, but the 1982 was praised by critics and made the estate's name. From 1991, when Valandraud in Saint-Émilion made its first vintage, a wave of tiny, dense, new oaked wines from sheds and garages followed; their makers were called garagistes, and Le Pin was named as their forerunner. The estate stayed small and never sought a rank: Pomerol has no classification. In 2011 a new cellar designed by Belgian architects opened on the site. Le Pin stands for the opulent side of Pomerol, the wine to pour when a guest wants pleasure young rather than in twenty years.
changed.why: The 1979 was raised in old barrels and malolactic in barrel began for want of tanks; the 1982 made the name; the garagistes are dated from 1991; the buyers are members of the family; the cellar of 2011 is the work of Belgian architects; the merchants of Britain and America are cut.

changed.was: The land of Cheval Blanc was once part of Château Figeac, whose owners sold vineyard from 1832 onwards. Through a marriage of 1852 it passed to the Fourcaud-Laussac family, who built the estate and held it for almost a century and a half; its name came, the story goes, from an old coaching inn where travellers changed horses. Medals won at the great exhibitions of the later nineteenth century were printed on the label. The 1947, picked in a scorching autumn, came out so ripe and dense that it is a vintage of history, talked of for its weight as a wine almost like Port. When Saint-Émilion drew up its first classification in 1955, Cheval Blanc and Ausone were the two estates ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé A, a rank they held alone until 2012. In 1998 the family sold the estate to two businessmen, and in 2011 a new cellar of concrete vats, one for each parcel, opened among the vines. In 2021 Cheval Blanc and Ausone withdrew from the classification, objecting to criteria that weighed marketing and tourism beside the wine in the glass. When a guest doubts that Cabernet Franc can lead a great Right Bank wine, Cheval Blanc is the answer to pour.
changed.now: The land of Cheval Blanc was once part of Château Figeac. In 1832 a judge of Libourne bought the heart of it, and more Figeac land followed over the next two decades. Through his daughter's marriage of 1852 it passed to the Laussac-Fourcaud family, later the Fourcaud-Laussac family, who held it until 1998; how it came by its name is not known for certain. It won a medal at the Universal Exhibition in London in 1862, which its label has carried ever since, and a gold medal at Paris in 1878. The 1947, made after an abnormally hot, dry summer, came out so ripe and dense that it is a vintage of history, talked of for its weight as a wine almost like Port. When Saint-Émilion drew up its first classification in 1955, Cheval Blanc and Ausone were the two estates ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé A, a rank they held alone until 2012. In June 2011 a new cellar of concrete vats, sized to the parcels, opened among the vines. changed.was: Ausonius (about 310 to about 395), the Latin poet of Bordeaux and tutor to the future emperor Gratian, wrote of his own vineyards, and local belief long held that his villa stood on this slope below the town, and the estate carries his name. The vines grow on the limestone côte, and the cellars run back into old quarries in the rock that once gave Saint-Émilion its building stone. When Saint-Émilion drew up its first classification in 1955, Ausone and Cheval Blanc were the two estates ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé A, a pair that held that rank alone for more than half a century. For much of that time the estate was shared between two branches of the owning family, and a long dispute between them ended in the mid 1990s, when one branch took sole charge of vineyard and cellar. Ausone kept its A rank in 2012, when Angélus and Pavie were raised to join it, but in 2021 it withdrew from the classification together with Cheval Blanc. Ausone is the voice of the limestone: cool, slow and built for the cellar, the opposite pole to Cheval Blanc's gravel.
changed.now: Ausonius (about 310 to about 395), the Latin poet of Bordeaux, tutor to the future emperor Gratian and the poet of the vines of the Moselle, gave the estate its name: local belief long held that his villa stood on this slope below the town, though no one has proved it. The vines grow on the limestone côte in an amphitheatre beneath the château, and the cellars run back into old quarry galleries cut into the rock. When Saint-Émilion drew up its first classification in 1955, Ausone and Cheval Blanc were the two estates ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé A, a pair that held that rank alone for more than half a century. For much of that time two families shared the estate, and a long dispute between them, which went to the courts, ended in the mid 1990s, when the Vauthier family bought the other half and took sole charge of vineyard and cellar. Ausone kept its A rank in 2012, when Angélus and Pavie were raised to join it, but in 2021 it withdrew from the classification, as Cheval Blanc did. Ausone is the voice of the limestone: cool, slow and built for the cellar, the opposite pole to Cheval Blanc's gravel.
changed.why: The Mosella in place of his own vineyards, the belief unproved, the quarry galleries, two families and the courts, the withdrawal as Cheval Blanc did rather than together.

changed.was: In the eighteenth century Figeac reached across much of the north west of Saint-Émilion, on gravel where, the story goes, a Gallo-Roman family whose name it carries had a villa in the second century. In the nineteenth century its owners sold off land, among it, from 1832, the parcels that became Cheval Blanc. In 1892 the estate was bought by the family of Thierry Manoncourt (1917 to 2010), who took charge of it in 1947 after training as an agronomist. He kept and widened the plantings of Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc on the warm gravel, so that Figeac grew into the Right Bank's Cabernet estate, closer in taste to the Médoc than to its Merlot neighbours. In 1955 it was ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé in Saint-Émilion's first classification, in the group below Ausone and Cheval Blanc, and it stayed in that group through every revision for more than sixty years. In 2022, with Ausone, Cheval Blanc and Angélus gone from the list, Figeac was promoted to A beside Pavie. Offer it to a guest who loves Pauillac: three grapes in near equal parts, cedar before plum.

In 1892 the grandparents of Thierry Manoncourt (1917 to 2010) bought the estate, and he took charge of it in 1947, as the estate tells it. He widened the plantings of Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc on the warm gravel and set the blend at about a third of each grape, so that Figeac grew into the Right Bank's Cabernet estate, closer in taste to the Médoc than to its Merlot neighbours. In 1955 it was ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé in Saint-Émilion's first classification, in the group below Ausone and Cheval Blanc, and it stayed in that group through every revision for more than sixty years. In 2022, with Ausone, Cheval Blanc and Angélus gone from the list, Figeac was promoted to A beside Pavie. Offer it to a guest who loves Pauillac: three grapes in near equal parts, cedar before plum.
